opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think transparency is one of the biggest unsolved problems in AI today, and TensorLogic addresses it almost for free, as a side effect of how it's built.

Look at where we are with deep learning. We have these enormously powerful models, but they're black boxes. You train a giant network, it does something impressive, and then you ask, "Why did it do that?" Nobody really knows. There's a whole field, mechanistic interpretability, of people painstakingly trying to reverse-engineer what these networks have learned. That's a sign something went wrong upstream. You built a thing you can't understand, and now you're doing archaeology on it.

In TensorLogic, the basic construct is the tensor equation, which is essentially the same thing as a logical rule. A Datalog rule saying "X is Y's grandparent if X is Z's parent and Z is Y's parent" is, under the hood, a tensor join followed by a projection, an Einstein summation. Once you see that, a neural network and a logic program aren't different species. They're written in the same language. So whatever the system knows, whether you put it in by hand or it was learned, is expressed as equations you can read. It's not smeared across a billion weights with no structure.

Then there's reasoning in embedding space. You can embed objects and relations and still reason over them, with a temperature parameter. At high temperature you get analogical, similarity-based generalization, the thing neural nets are good at. As you lower the temperature it becomes more and more like strict deduction, and at zero it is pure deductive logic. So you can dial the system toward exactly the regime where every conclusion can be traced back through a chain of rules. That's transparency and reliability together. No hallucinations in that regime, because the system can't conclude something that doesn't follow.

Why does this matter so much? Three reasons.

First, trust. If AI is going to make decisions in medicine, law, finance, or science, people will reasonably demand to know why. "The network said so" isn't an acceptable answer, and it shouldn't be.

Second, debugging and improvement. If you can see the rules, you can see when one is wrong and fix it. With a black box you mostly retrain and hope.

Third, and this is underappreciated, the interaction between humans and the system. If knowledge is in a readable form, a human expert can contribute rules, and the system can hand learned knowledge back in a form the expert can inspect, criticize, and build on. That's a real collaboration, not the human feeding data into a machine and getting an oracle out.

So transparency isn't a nice extra. If we want AI that's powerful and also something we can understand, control, and trust, then the representation has to be one that both learning and reasoning can operate on, and that humans can read. That's what TensorLogic is trying to be.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think transparency is the thing that's missing most from AI today, and it's not a cosmetic problem, it's a fundamental one. The way we build systems now, you have a neural network with billions of weights, and nobody, including the people who trained it, can tell you why it produced a given output. It's a black box. And then on top of that black box we bolt on all these ad hoc things, chain of thought, retrieval, guardrails, and each one is its own opaque layer. So we're stacking black boxes on black boxes and calling it progress.

What TensorLogic does is collapse all of that into one thing. The key insight is that a logical rule and a tensor operation, an Einstein summation, are actually the same object. A rule in logic says, if these facts hold, then this conclusion follows. That's a join followed by a projection. And a join followed by a projection is exactly what einsum computes. So once you see that, the whole system, the learning, the reasoning, the knowledge, is expressed in a single language, and every step of a computation corresponds to something you can read off as a logical inference.

That's why I say transparency isn't a feature we added, it falls out of the design. If your model is made of rules that happen to be tensors, then when it reaches a conclusion you can trace exactly which facts and which rules it used to get there. You can inspect them, you can edit them, you can prove things about them. Compare that to trying to interpret a transformer by poking at attention heads after the fact. That's archaeology. TensorLogic is more like having the blueprints.

And there's a deeper point here, which is about hallucination. The reason language models hallucinate is that they have no mechanism that distinguishes "this is a valid inference" from "this sounds plausible." Everything is just statistics over tokens. In TensorLogic you have a knob, essentially, where you can run the reasoning in a strict mode, where only sound deductions go through, or you can relax it and let it generalize, be more like a neural network, do analogy. But crucially you know which mode you're in, and you know where the uncertainty is coming from. So transparency isn't just about satisfying regulators or making people feel better. It's what lets you actually control the system, debug it, trust it in domains like medicine or law where a confident wrong answer is dangerous.

I'd also say this matters for scientific reasons. We've spent a decade getting better results with systems we understand less and less. That's not a sustainable trajectory for a science. Physics didn't progress by building more elaborate machines no one could explain. It progressed by finding the unifying principles. TensorLogic is my attempt at that for AI, and transparency is really the proof that the unification worked, because if you've genuinely found the right abstraction, the system should be legible.

astra-6.text:
Because we want to understand what a model has learned, not just observe that it produces good predictions. With a neural network, the knowledge is distributed across weights, and it can be very difficult to see why a particular answer follows. Logic gives us a language for expressing that knowledge in terms of relationships and rules.

The idea with TensorLogic is to bring those two things together: the ability to learn using tensors and the ability to express computations in logical terms. That gives us a way to inspect what the system is doing, question its assumptions, and potentially correct it.

Now, having a logical representation doesn’t automatically make a large model easy to understand. But it gives us a basis for understanding it. And that matters for debugging, for scientific discovery, and for deciding when we should trust the output. We want systems whose knowledge we can examine and improve, as well as systems that perform well.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if you want to trust a system, you need to be able to understand what it’s doing. With a neural network, you have all these weights, and it’s very difficult to see why it arrived at a particular answer. With logic, you can inspect the rules and follow the reasoning. The idea of TensorLogic is to bring those two things together, so that learning and reasoning happen in a common language.

That gives you a way to examine what the system has learned, identify where it’s going wrong, and potentially correct it. And transparency doesn’t mean that a huge model suddenly becomes easy to understand. But having an explicit logical interpretation gives you a much better starting point for explaining and debugging it.
